latin: Inter dementes<sup>1</sup>. — Cui scribis, o bone? — Mihi!
Quomodo scire possum, cum epistulam nondum acceperim<sup>2</sup>?
Professor. — Quis hoc dixit: «Venio ut Caesarem sepeliam<sup>3</sup>»?
Cum venum mihi hunc canem dedisti<sup>5</sup>, latronibus optimum eum esse dixisti...
sed superiore<sup>6</sup> nocte latrones domum meam, ut furarentur, ingressi sunt<sup>7</sup>,
neque unum quidem ex iis momordit<sup>8</sup>.
Latronibus esse optimum jam tibi dixi!
Centurio<sup>9</sup> quidam coram militibus contionem<sup>10</sup> habet quibus haec explanat: «Patria est mater nostra...»
Postea Josepho. — Quid est patria, Josephe?
In nosocomio<sup>11</sup>: Rector. — Aegrotus quem nunc de tecto<sup>12</sup> vides pendentem dicit se esse lucernam.
Rector. — Quia in posterum sine luce<sup>15</sup> erimus.
english: [A story of] (among) madmen. — Who are you writing to, my good fellow? — To me!
And what are you writing to yourself?
How can I know, since I haven't yet received the letter?
The teacher. — Who said this: «I come (so that I may) bury Caesar»?
The pupil. — The undertaker, of course!
When you sold me this dog, you told me [it] was excellent for thieves...
but last night, thieves entered my house to burgle,
and it didn't even bite [a single one] of them.
I already told you that it was very good for thieves!
A captain [assembles his soldiers] (a gathering in presence — before — of the soldiers), to whom he explains this: «The fatherland is our mother...»
Then he questions one of the soldiers:
What is the fatherland, Antoine?
Antoine. — The fatherland is my mother.
Then, to Joseph. — What is the fatherland, Joseph?
Joseph. — It's Antoine's mother!
At the hospital: The director. — The patient you see [hanging] (hanging) from the roof says that he is a lantern.
The visitor. — Why don't you take him down (you)?
The director. — Because afterwards, we would be without light.

footnotes: Mens, mentis, f., mind, intelligence; whence the adjectives demens and amens, deprived of mind, that is to say mad.
Acceperim, -is, -it, etc.: perfect of the subjunctive of accipere.
Sepelio, -is, -ire, ivi or ii, sepultum, to bury (here, in the subj. after ut); sepultura, burial; sepulcrum, the tomb.
Libitina was the goddess who presided over burials, whence libitinarius, -ii, m., the undertaker.
Venum dare (or vendere, -o, -is, -ere, vendidi, venditum), to sell; veneo, -is, -ire, ivi or ii, venitum, to be sold: Haec raeda 8 000 francis veniit, this car was sold for 8,000 francs.
Superior, -ior, -ius: comparative of superus, -a, -um, from above (superlative, supremus, -a, -um, cf. L. 48, song).
Ingredior, -eris, -i, ingressus sum = in + gradior, to enter.
To which verb does momordit belong? Answer: R. and N. 63, 2 B.
Centurio, -onis, m., Centurion, officer commanding 100 men.
Tectum, -i, n., the roof; like tegmen (L. 48, N. 3) comes from tegere.
Mitto, -is, -ere, misi, missum, to send. Think of the Missi Dominici of Charlemagne. Missio, -onis, f., the fact of sending, the mission. Demittere, to send from above, to bring down.
comments: Phalerae, -arum, f. pl., military decorations, or metal ornaments of horses' harnesses.

Circensis, -e, adj., relating to the circus; circus, -i, m., usually designates the hippodrome, sometimes the arena where gladiators fought (ordinarily called amphitheatrum). — Mappa, -ae, f., napkin which was thrown to give the start of the games. — Acer, acris, acre, sharp, cutting; here spirited, refers to equus. Meta, -ae, f., the turning post, beyond which one must turn. — Quadrigae, -arum, f. pl., chariot drawn by four horses; a chariot with two horses is likewise called bigae. These two words are generally used in the plural, even if there is only one chariot. — Cruor, -oris, m., the blood that flows from a wound; blood in general is called sanguis, -inis, m.

english: From the consul's hand
— the signal has fallen,
— spirited with the chariot
— the horse leaps.
Behind us resound
— the gates of the [boxes] (prisons).
— How [we love] the [games] of the circus (delight)!
— How the charioteers rejoice!
There stands the turning post;
— turn the four-horse chariot(s).
— He who does not avoid [the post]
— breaks [his] wheels.
The horses collide,
— the crash rises to the sky;
— the chariots rush on, mingled,
— everywhere [flows] (is made) the blood.
Refrain: They jingle, they jingle
— always the harnesses.
— How willingly they hear
— the charioteers in the race.
song.source: From Carmina Latina (a Centaur Books, Slough, Anglia, editis). Music by J. Pierpoint (Jingle Bells). Latin words by T. W. Melluish. Record and collection published by Centaur Books, Slough (England).
